questions.q: Sunita does 90 J of work by pushing a box with a constant force of 45 N, always in the direction of the push. The box is displaced ___ m.

Raju leans on the compound wall of his school with a steady push of 300 N for ten minutes and sweats. His friend says, 'You did 300 N x 600 s of work on the wall.' What is the work done by Raju on the wall?
questions.a: Zero, because the wall is not displaced in the direction of the push. Work needs displacement (s = 0 gives W = 0), however large the force; Raju feels tired because his muscles use up internal energy.
o: Zero, because the wall is not displaced in the direction of the push
180000 J, because force multiplied by time gives work
300 J, because the force of 300 N acts on the wall for 1 m
Negative, because the wall pushes back on Raju as hard as he pushes it

questions.q: Latha carries an 8 kg box along a level corridor 20 m long, keeping it at the same height. Take g = 10 m/s squared. How much work does her upward supporting force do on the box?
questions.a: 0 J, because the upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement. The supporting force is upward and the box moves horizontally, so there is no displacement along the force.
o: 0 J, because the upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement
1600 J, because the force 80 N acts over the displacement of 20 m
160 J, because her force equals the 8 kg mass over the 20 m
-1600 J, because she must work against the weight of the box

questions.q: A trolley is pulled 6 m forward by a horizontal force of 35 N while friction of 15 N acts against the motion over the same 6 m. What is the total work done on the trolley by these two forces together?
questions.a: 120 J. Pull: +35 N x 6 m = +210 J; friction: -15 N x 6 m = -90 J; total = 120 J.
o: 210 J, found from the pull alone
90 J, found from the friction alone
300 J, found by adding 35, 15 and 6 and multiplying

questions.q: In which of these tasks does the person do negative work on the object?
questions.a: A mason slowly lowers a loaded bucket by a rope to the ground. While lowering, the rope's upward force opposes the downward displacement, so the work is negative.
o: A mason slowly lowers a loaded bucket by a rope to the ground
A mason hauls the loaded bucket up from the ground with the same rope
A porter pushes a trolley forward along a level railway platform steadily
A porter carries a heavy bag steadily along a level railway platform

questions.q: A student claims the work done by the person is zero in each of four tasks. In which task is the claim wrong?
questions.a: Lifting a 5 kg bag slowly through 1 m onto a shelf. Lifting gives W = 50 N x 1 m = 50 J, which is not zero; the other three have s = 0 or a force perpendicular to the displacement.
o: Lifting a 5 kg bag slowly through 1 m onto a shelf
Holding the 5 kg bag steady at shoulder height for a minute
Carrying the 5 kg bag at constant height along a level lane
Pushing hard on a rigid wall while holding the 5 kg bag

questions.q:
Statement 1: A force of 10 N acting on an object that is displaced 5 m always does 50 J of work on it.
Statement 2: The work done by a force on an object can be negative.
Statement 3: A person who pushes a rigid wall and feels tired has done work on the wall.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only. Statement 1 fails when the force is perpendicular to the displacement (zero) or opposite to it (-50 J); statement 3 fails since the wall does not move.
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When a block slides across a rough floor, the work done on the block by friction is negative.
Reason (R): Friction always acts in the direction of the block's displacement.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Friction acts opposite to the displacement, which is exactly why its work is negative, so R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A goalkeeper's hand moves back 25 cm while it stops a ball with a constant force of 180 N.
(a) Calculate the work done by the goalkeeper on the ball.
(b) State the sign of the work done by the ball on the goalkeeper's hand and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) -45 J. (b) Positive, because the ball pushes the hand in the same direction as the hand moves.
s: Part (b): positive, as the ball's force on the hand and the hand's displacement are in the same direction

questions.q:
A labourer lifts a 5 kg bag slowly from the floor to a shelf 2 m high, applying an upward force equal to its weight. Take g = 10 m/s squared.
(a) Find the work done by the labourer.
(b) He lifts 4 such bags together to the same shelf. Find the work done.
s: Part (b): force is 4 times larger over the same distance, so 400 J

questions.q: True or False? Since 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2, a joule can also be written as 1 kg m^2 s^-2. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. 1 J = 1 N x 1 m = 1 kg m s^-2 x 1 m = 1 kg m^2 s^-2.
s: Reason: substitute 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2 into 1 J = 1 N x 1 m

questions.q: Differentiate between negative work and zero work done by a person on a dumbbell, giving one exercise situation for each.
questions.a: Negative work: the force and displacement are opposite, e.g. slowly lowering the dumbbell. Zero work: the dumbbell is not displaced along the force, e.g. holding it still.
s: Negative work: force opposite to displacement, with a situation such as lowering the dumbbell
Zero work: no displacement (or a perpendicular force), with a situation such as holding it still

questions.q:
A force-displacement graph for a trolley is a flat horizontal line at 12 N from a displacement of 0 to 0.5 m (the force is in the direction of motion).
(a) Find the work done using the area under the line.
(b) How would you find the work if the force were not constant?
questions.a: (a) 6 J. (b) By finding the area under the force-displacement graph between the initial and final positions.
s: Part (a): area of rectangle 12 N x 0.5 m = 6 J
Part (b): the area under the force-displacement graph still gives the work

questions.q: Kavya says, 'I carried a bucket of water 50 m along a level lane with an upward force of 80 N, so I did 80 N x 50 m = 4000 J of work on the bucket.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. Her upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so the work done by it is 0 J.
s: Reason: the force is perpendicular to the displacement, so no displacement along the force

questions.q: Show that a person lowering a 20 kg bucket slowly into a well 12 m deep cannot be doing positive work on the bucket, and find the work done by the person. Take g = 10 m/s squared.
questions.a: The person's upward force opposes the downward displacement, so the work is negative: -2400 J.
s: Force upward equals the weight 200 N while the displacement is downward
Opposite directions mean the work cannot be positive

questions.q: The work done by a force on an object is -60 J. Write a situation, with the force and the displacement, in which this happens, and say how you know the sign is negative.
questions.a: E.g. a cyclist's brake applies 30 N against the motion while the cycle moves 2 m forward: W = 30 N x (-2 m) = -60 J.
s: A realistic situation with force and displacement values
Force and displacement in opposite directions, so negative
Product of the stated values equals -60 J

questions.q: A 4 kg book is lifted slowly from the floor to a shelf 1.2 m high, held there for 30 s, then lowered slowly onto a table 0.7 m above the floor. The person's force always equals the weight of the book. Take g = 10 m/s squared. Find the work done by the person (i) while lifting, (ii) while holding, (iii) while lowering, (iv) in all, and (v) check (iv) by one multiplication.
s: Lowering 0.5 m: 40 N x (-0.5 m) = -20 J
Check: the net displacement is 0.7 m upward, and 40 N x 0.7 m = 28 J

questions.q: Rani pushes an almirah with 400 N for two minutes but it does not move. Meena pushes a chair with 40 N through 5 m along the floor, in the direction of her push. (i) Find the work done by Rani on the almirah. (ii) Find the work done by Meena on the chair. (iii) Who did more work on the object? (iv) Why does Rani still feel tired? (v) What must happen for Rani to be doing work on the almirah?
questions.a: (i) 0 J (ii) 200 J (iii) Meena (iv) Rani's muscles keep contracting and use up the body's internal energy (v) the almirah must be displaced in the direction of her push
s: Rani: displacement is zero, so 0 J
Meena did more work on the object it acted on
Tiredness: muscles repeatedly expand and contract and use internal energy even when no work is done on the almirah
Work needs displacement along the force, so the almirah must move in the direction of the push

questions.q:
At a grain godown in Warangal, 50 kg sacks are lifted onto a truck bed 1.5 m high. Take g = 10 m/s squared and let each lifting force equal the weight lifted. Ramesh lifts the sacks one at a time and loads 12 sacks. Suresh lifts two sacks together on each trip and also loads 12 sacks. The contractor wants to pay by the work done on the sacks in the scientific sense.
(a) Find the work done by Ramesh in lifting one sack.
(b) Find the total work done by Ramesh and by Suresh.
(c) A labourer then walks 8 m along the truck bed carrying a sack at constant height. Find the work done by his supporting force.
(d) Should the contractor pay Ramesh and Suresh equally on this basis? Name one fair factor besides work done on the sacks.
questions.a: (a) 750 J (b) 9000 J each (c) 0 J (d) Yes, equal pay by this measure; a fair extra factor is the number of trips or the strain of a larger force.
s: Ramesh 12 x 750 = 9000 J; Suresh 6 x 1500 = 9000 J
0 J: the supporting force is perpendicular to the level displacement
Equal on this measure (9000 J each), with a reasoned extra factor such as trips made or force handled

questions.q:
In a gym in Nagpur, Asha lifts a 12 kg dumbbell slowly from the floor to a height of 0.9 m, holds it still for 5 s, then lowers it slowly back to the floor. Her force always equals the weight of the dumbbell (g = 10 m/s squared). Her coach says, 'The dumbbell ends where it began, so you did no work and the exercise is useless.'
(a) Find the work done by Asha while lifting.
(b) Find the work done while she holds it still.
(c) Find the work done while lowering, and the total for the whole exercise.
(d) Judge the coach's statement: say which part is right and which part is not.
questions.a: (a) 108 J (b) 0 J (c) -108 J; total 0 J (d) Partly right: the net work on the dumbbell is zero, but her muscles use up internal energy in all three phases, so the exercise is not useless.
s: Net work is zero (right) but muscles use internal energy in every phase (so 'useless' is not justified)

questions.q: A ball at rest in a fielder's hand gets 45 J of work from the throw. Later the wicketkeeper's gloves do -45 J of work on it as they stop it. Ignoring all losses, the ball's final kinetic energy is ___ J.
Anil eats a banana, swings his arm to ring the school bell, and the bell is heard across the ground. Which sequence names the forms of energy in the order they appear?
questions.a: Chemical, then mechanical, then sound. Food energy powers the muscles (mechanical), and the ringing bell converts mechanical energy into sound.
o: Chemical, then mechanical, then sound
Chemical, then sound, then mechanical
Mechanical, then chemical, then sound
Thermal, then mechanical, then sound

questions.q: A steel spoon at 25 C is dipped into tea at 80 C without anyone doing mechanical work on it. Which statement about energy is correct?
questions.a: Energy flows as heat from the tea to the spoon until they are at the same temperature. Energy can be transferred as heat when objects at different temperatures touch, from the hotter to the colder one.
o: Energy flows as heat from the tea to the spoon until they are at the same temperature
No energy moves at all, because no mechanical work was done on the spoon by anyone
Energy flows from the spoon to the tea, since steel holds more energy
Energy flows from tea to spoon only if the spoon is stirred through the tea

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a correct statement of the work-energy theorem as developed in this chapter?
questions.a: It holds only when the forces acting on the object are constant. The chapter states that the theorem also holds when the forces applied are not constant.
o: It holds only when the forces acting on the object are constant
Work done on an object appears as a change in its energy
It can be applied to a system of objects as well as to one object
Positive work done on an object increases its energy

questions.q: In a carrom shot the moving striker hits a white coin. Which pair of statements about the work done at this collision is correct?
questions.a: The striker does positive work on the coin, and the coin does negative work on the striker. The forces are equal and opposite; the coin moves along the striker's force and the striker moves against the coin's force.
o: The striker does positive work on the coin, and the coin does negative work on the striker
The striker does negative work on the coin, and the coin does positive work on the striker
Both the striker and the coin do positive work on each other
Neither does any work, since the two objects only touch for an instant of time

questions.q: A moving trolley has 60 J of kinetic energy. A rough patch does -25 J of work on it. What is its kinetic energy afterwards?
questions.a: 35 J. Change in energy = work done = -25 J, so 60 J - 25 J = 35 J.

questions.q:
Statement 1: Energy can be transferred from a hot object to a cold one as heat, without any mechanical work being done.
Statement 2: Energy can be transferred from one object to another only when the objects touch.
Statement 3: The SI unit of energy is the same as the SI unit of work.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: the Sun's energy reaches the Earth by radiation, and energy is also carried by sound waves and in electric circuits.
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The work done in raising a flowerpot to a height appears as kinetic energy of the pot.
Reason (R): Work done on an object appears as a change in its energy.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Work done on the pot raises its potential energy, not kinetic energy, while R is the work-energy theorem.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with the energy change taking place (column II).
Column I: 1. A mess cook switches on an electric water heater  2. A student strikes the school gong  3. A runner's legs speed up after lunch  4. A bulb glows in the hall
Column II: a. chemical to mechanical  b. electrical to light  c. mechanical to sound  d. electrical to thermal
questions.a: 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b. The heater gives thermal energy, the gong sound, the runner's muscles mechanical energy from food, and the bulb light.

questions.q:
A moving striker has 5 J of energy and hits a white coin, giving it 3 J (ignore losses).
(a) State the work done by the striker on the coin.
(b) State the work done by the coin on the striker and the striker's energy afterwards.
questions.a: (a) +3 J. (b) -3 J; the striker is left with 2 J.
s: Part (a): +3 J, equal to the energy gained by the coin
Part (b): -3 J by the coin, so 5 - 3 = 2 J remains

questions.q:
Arjun lifts a 2 kg flowerpot slowly from the floor to a shelf 1.5 m high. Take g = 10 m/s squared.
(a) Find the work done by Arjun.
(b) By the work-energy theorem, state the energy gained by the pot and its form.
questions.a: (a) 30 J. (b) 30 J of gravitational potential energy.
s: Part (b): energy gained = 30 J, stored as potential energy

questions.q: True or False? If no work is done on an object, the work-energy theorem says its energy must be zero. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The theorem says the change in energy is zero, so the object keeps whatever energy it already had.
s: Correction: no work means no change in energy, not zero energy

questions.q: Differentiate between transferring energy by doing work and transferring it as heat, with one example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: Work: a force displaces the object, e.g. the ball hitting the wickets and moving them. Heat: energy flows from a hotter to a colder object in contact.
s: Work transfer: force and displacement, with an example
Heat transfer: between objects at different temperatures, with an example

questions.q: Explain how positive work and negative work done on an object differ in what they do to its energy, with one example of each.
questions.a: Positive work increases the object's energy (the fielder throwing a ball); negative work decreases it (the goalkeeper stopping the ball).
s: Positive work raises energy, with an example
Negative work lowers energy, with an example

questions.q: Divya says, 'The work-energy theorem tells us that work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy.' Is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. Work equals the change in the object's energy, which may be kinetic energy but may also be potential energy, as when a pot is raised.
s: The change may be in potential energy, e.g. a pot raised to a height
Correct statement: work done = change in its energy

questions.q: A trolley has 40 J of energy and only positive work of 15 J is done on it by the forces acting. Show that its energy cannot become 25 J, and state what it becomes.
questions.a: Positive work raises the energy, so the energy is 40 J + 15 J = 55 J and cannot be 25 J.
s: Work done equals the change in energy
Positive work means an increase, so a fall to 25 J is impossible

questions.q: Write a carrom-like situation in which one object does +4 J of work on another. State the work done by the second on the first and the change in energy of each.
questions.a: E.g. a striker does +4 J on a coin; the coin does -4 J on the striker; the coin gains 4 J and the striker loses 4 J.
s: A situation with +4 J of work by the first object
The second object does -4 J on the first

questions.q: A fielder eats lunch, throws a ball that hits the wickets, and the wickets move. Describe the energy changes in order, using the terms chemical energy, mechanical energy, positive work, negative work and the work-energy theorem.
questions.a: Food energy becomes mechanical energy in muscles; the fielder does positive work on the ball, which gains energy equal to that work; the ball does positive work on the wickets; the wickets do negative work on the ball, lowering its energy.
s: Chemical energy of food to mechanical energy in the muscles
Fielder does positive work on the ball
Ball gains energy equal to the work (work-energy theorem)
Ball does positive work on the wickets, transferring energy
Wickets do negative work on the ball, so the ball's energy falls

questions.q: A striker with 6 J of energy gives 4 J to a white coin. The white coin then hits a black coin and gives it 2.5 J. Ignoring losses, find (i) the work done by the striker on the white coin, (ii) the striker's energy left, (iii) the work done by the white coin on the striker, (iv) the white coin's energy after its collision, and (v) the work done by the black coin on the white coin.
s: +4 J, equal to the energy gained

questions.q:
A bowler does 92 J of work on a ball that starts at rest in his hand (ignore air). The ball then hits the stumps and gives 30 J of energy to them, and carries on. The wicketkeeper stops the ball by moving his gloves backward with a constant force.
(a) Find the energy gained by the ball in the delivery.
(b) State the work done by the ball on the stumps and by the stumps on the ball.
(c) Find the work the keeper's gloves must do to stop the ball, with sign.
(d) The gloves can move back 0.5 m or 1.0 m while stopping it. Compare the force in the two cases and say which the keeper should prefer.
questions.a: (a) 92 J (b) +30 J and -30 J (c) -62 J (d) 124 N for 0.5 m and 62 N for 1.0 m; the longer movement halves the force, so prefer 1.0 m.
s: 92 J, equal to the work done
+30 J by the ball, -30 J by the stumps
Energy left 92 - 30 = 62 J, so -62 J by the gloves
Force = 62 J / distance: 124 N or 62 N; the longer movement gives the smaller force

questions.q:
In a lab in Nashik, Kavya pulls a 2 kg trolley from rest along a smooth track. The force shown by a spring balance rises steadily from 0 N to 12 N over the first 3 m, then stays at 12 N for the next 1.5 m, always along the motion.
(a) Find the work done in the first 3 m using the area under the force-displacement graph.
(b) Find the work done in the next 1.5 m.
(c) State the trolley's energy at 4.5 m.
(d) Kavya wants 72 J. Plan 1 doubles only the length of the 12 N stretch to 3 m; Plan 2 doubles the force at every point. Which plan gives exactly 72 J? Show it.
questions.a: (a) 18 J (b) 18 J (c) 36 J (d) Plan 2: 2 x 36 = 72 J; Plan 1 gives 18 + 36 = 54 J.
s: Starts from rest, so energy = 36 J
Plan 1 gives 18 + 12 x 3 = 54 J; Plan 2 doubles every work, giving 72 J

questions.q: A trolley of 2 kg moves at 3 m/s. If its speed is raised to 9 m/s with the mass unchanged, its kinetic energy becomes ___ times the original.
A truck has 4 times the mass of a car and moves at half the car's speed. What is the ratio of the kinetic energy of the truck to that of the car?
questions.a: 1 : 1. Truck: 1/2 x 4m x (v/2)^2 = 1/2 m v^2, the same as the car.

questions.q: A cyclist and cycle together have a mass of 60 kg and move at 18 km/h. What is the kinetic energy?
questions.a: 750 J. 18 km/h = 5 m/s, so K = 1/2 x 60 x 25 = 750 J; 9720 J comes from using 18 without converting.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes and stops in 50 m under a constant braking force. What is the force?
questions.a: 4000 N. The work done by the brakes equals the initial kinetic energy, 200000 J, and 200000 J / 50 m = 4000 N.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about kinetic energy is NOT correct?
questions.a: Two cars of equal mass and speed moving in opposite directions have equal and opposite kinetic energies. Kinetic energy has no direction, so both cars have the same positive kinetic energy.
o: Two cars of equal mass and speed moving in opposite directions have equal and opposite kinetic energies
The kinetic energy of an object moving with constant velocity does not change as it changes position
Doubling the velocity of a vehicle makes its kinetic energy exactly 4 times as large
Negative work done on an object that slows it decreases its kinetic energy

questions.q:
Statement 1: An object moving with constant velocity keeps the same kinetic energy as it changes position.
Statement 2: Negative work done on a moving object that slows it down decreases its kinetic energy.
Statement 3: Work done on an object that speeds up from u to v equals 1/2 m (v^2 - u^2).
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements. All three follow from the work-energy theorem and the derivation of K = 1/2 mv^2.
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A 1500 kg car moving at 10 m/s has more kinetic energy than a 0.2 kg ball moving at 43 m/s.
Reason (R): Kinetic energy has no direction.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Car: 75000 J; ball: 184.9 J, so A is true; R is also true but it is the mass and the square of the speed, not directionlessness, that give the comparison.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Match each change (column I) with its effect on kinetic energy (column II).
Column I: 1. speed tripled, mass unchanged  2. mass tripled, speed unchanged  3. speed halved, mass unchanged  4. mass doubled and speed halved
Column II: a. 9 times  b. 3 times  c. one-fourth  d. one-half
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d. Kinetic energy varies with mass and with the square of the speed: 3^2 = 9, 3, (1/2)^2 = 1/4, and 2 x 1/4 = 1/2.

questions.q:
A bowler delivers a 0.16 kg ball at 90 km/h.
(a) Express the speed in m/s.
(b) Find the kinetic energy of the ball.

A school bus of mass 6000 kg moves at 10 m/s.
(a) Find its kinetic energy.
(b) At what speed would its kinetic energy be 4 times as large?
s: Part (b): 4 times the energy needs 2 times the speed, 20 m/s

questions.q: True or False? A ball rolling at a steady 5 m/s has more kinetic energy at the far end of the field than at the start. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. With constant velocity its kinetic energy does not change with position.
s: Correction: K = 1/2 mv^2 depends only on mass and speed, which are unchanged

questions.q: Name the two relations that are combined to derive the work done on an object that goes from speed u to speed v, and give the result for u = 0.
questions.a: W = F x s with F = ma, and v^2 - u^2 = 2as, give W = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2); for u = 0 this is K = 1/2 mv^2.
s: The two relations: W = F x s with F = ma, and v^2 = u^2 + 2as
Result W = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2), so K = 1/2 mv^2 when u = 0

questions.q:
Two objects A and B have masses 2m and 8m and the same kinetic energy.
(a) Which moves faster?
(b) Find the ratio of the speeds vA : vB.
questions.a: (a) A, the lighter one. (b) 2 : 1.
s: Part (a): the lighter object A, as K depends on mass and speed squared
Part (b): 2m vA^2 = 8m vB^2 gives vA : vB = 2 : 1

questions.q: Neha says, 'The 40 J of work I did pushing a 5 kg cart from rest gives it a speed of 4 m/s.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes. K = 40 J, so 1/2 x 5 x v^2 = 40 gives v = 4 m/s.
s: Work equals the kinetic energy gained, 40 J, as it starts from rest

questions.q: A shopkeeper says a 0.5 kg ball moving at 3 m/s has 4 J of kinetic energy. Show that this is impossible and state the speed needed for 4 J.
questions.a: At 3 m/s, K = 1/2 x 0.5 x 9 = 2.25 J, not 4 J. For 4 J, v^2 = 16, so v = 4 m/s.
s: 2.25 J is not 4 J, so the claim is impossible

questions.q: Write a situation in which a moving object has 90 J of kinetic energy, giving its mass and speed, and check it.
questions.a: E.g. a 5 kg trolley at 6 m/s: 1/2 x 5 x 36 = 90 J (or a 20 kg bag at 3 m/s).
s: A realistic object with mass and speed

questions.q: A jet of mass 12000 kg lands at 60 m/s and is stopped by a wire exerting a constant backward force of 270000 N. Find the distance in which it stops.
s: Initial kinetic energy 1/2 x 12000 x 3600 = 21600000 J
Work by the wire = -F x s equals the change in kinetic energy

questions.q: A jet aircraft of mass 20000 kg is stopped within 80 m by a wire exerting a constant backward force of 450000 N. (i) State the sign of the work done by the wire. (ii) Write the change in kinetic energy. (iii) Equate it to the work done. (iv) Find the landing speed in m/s. (v) Convert it to km/h.
s: Force opposite to displacement, so the work is negative
Change in K = 0 - 1/2 x 20000 x v^2

questions.q: A 1000 kg car is braked by a constant force of 5000 N. Compare a city road limit of 10 m/s with a highway speed of 20 m/s: (i) find the kinetic energy at each speed, (ii) find the stopping distance at each, (iii) state by what factor the distance grows when the speed doubles, and (iv) explain why, and (v) say what this means for a driver.
questions.a: (i) 50000 J and 200000 J (ii) 10 m and 40 m (iii) 4 times (iv) K varies as v^2 and the distance equals K divided by the force (v) doubling the speed needs four times the room to stop
s: Distance grows 4 times for 2 times the speed
Reason: K is proportional to v^2 and s = K / F for a constant force
Conclusion: keep far more distance at higher speed

questions.q:
A cricket coach in Vijayawada compares the kinetic energy of deliveries of a 0.16 kg ball. A junior bowls at 25 m/s and a senior at 35 m/s. The wicketkeeper's gloves move back 0.4 m while stopping the senior's ball.
(a) Find the kinetic energy of each delivery.
(b) Find the average force on the ball from the gloves in stopping the senior's ball.
(c) Plan X lets the gloves move back 0.8 m. Plan Y asks the senior to bowl at 30 m/s with gloves moving 0.4 m. Find the force for each plan.
(d) Which plan gives the smaller force on the keeper's hands, and what is the cost of each?
questions.a: (a) 50 J and 98 J (b) 245 N (c) 122.5 N and 180 N (d) Plan X, at the cost of a bigger glove movement; Plan Y costs the bowler pace.
s: Plan X gives the smaller force; X costs room to move the gloves, Y costs pace

questions.q:
A tanker lorry on a highway near Nellore has a mass of 8000 kg when empty and 12500 kg when full. Both travel at 10 m/s, and its brakes give a constant force of 40000 N.
(a) Find the kinetic energy when empty and when full.
(b) Find the stopping distance in each case.
(c) At what speed must the full tanker travel to stop in the same distance as the empty one?
(d) The authority can either limit full tankers to that speed or require brakes strong enough to stop in the same distance at 10 m/s. Find that brake force and recommend one option with a reason.
questions.a: (a) 400000 J and 625000 J (b) 10 m and 15.625 m (c) 8 m/s (28.8 km/h) (d) 62500 N; either, with reasoning.
s: Brake force 625000 / 10 = 62500 N; a reasoned recommendation (speed limit is cheap, stronger brakes keep traffic speed)

questions.q: A 2 kg pot on a balcony 6 m above the ground is carried up to a terrace 9 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s squared, its potential energy rises by ___ J.
In Activity 7.1 a heavy ball is dropped onto a bed of loose sand from 1 m, from 2 m and from 3 m, at three different spots. Where is the depression deepest, and why?
questions.a: From 3 m, because raising the ball higher takes more work, so it holds more potential energy. The greater the height above the Earth's surface, the greater the potential energy, which creates a deeper depression.
o: From 3 m, because raising the ball higher takes more work, so it holds more potential energy
From 1 m, because the ball spends longer at that spot and so digs in deeper
From 3 m, because the ball's mass increases as it is raised higher
The three depressions are equal because the ball's mass is the same

questions.q: A child slides down a frictionless slide that is 1.8 m high. With g = 10 m/s squared, what is her speed at the bottom?
questions.a: 6 m/s. mgh = 1/2 mv^2 gives v = square root of (2 x 10 x 1.8) = 6 m/s; the mass cancels.
o: 6 m/s
18 m/s
36 m/s

questions.q: On Earth Anil throws a ball up and it reaches 5 m. An astronaut on the Moon, where gravity is one-sixth of that on Earth, throws it up with the same speed. How high does it go?
questions.a: 30 m. The same kinetic energy equals mgh, and with g one-sixth the height is 6 times larger.
o: 6 m

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT happen to a ball falling freely from rest through the air, when air resistance can be ignored?
questions.a: Its mechanical energy increases as its kinetic energy increases. Mechanical energy is conserved: what the potential energy loses the kinetic energy gains.
o: Its mechanical energy increases as its kinetic energy increases
Its potential energy decreases as it falls
Its kinetic energy increases by exactly the amount its potential energy decreases
Its mechanical energy stays equal to mgh of the starting point

questions.q: In Activity 7.2 a pendulum bob is released level with a marked line, but after two swings it only reaches slightly below the line. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: Some mechanical energy is lost to friction at the support and to air resistance. Without such losses the bob would reach nearly the same height again.
o: Some mechanical energy is lost to friction at the support and to air resistance
Gravity becomes weaker and weaker as the bob swings to and fro many times
The potential energy of the bob changes into mass
The bob gains kinetic energy at the lowest point and keeps all of it for ever

questions.q:
Statement 1: The expression U = mgh can be used for a satellite at any height above the Earth.
Statement 2: The energy stored in a ball-Earth system when they are separated is due to their relative positions.
Statement 3: A ball moving horizontally at constant velocity near the ground has no change in its gravitational potential energy.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only. U = mgh holds only near the Earth's surface where g is nearly constant, so statement 1 is false.
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The speed of a child at the bottom of a frictionless slide depends only on the height of the slide, not on her mass or the shape of the slide.
Reason (R): Her potential energy mgh at the top is converted entirely into kinetic energy 1/2 mv^2 at the bottom, so v is the square root of 2gh.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The mass cancels in mgh = 1/2 mv^2, leaving v dependent on h alone.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Match each object (column I) with its potential energy above the ground (column II). Take g = 10 m/s squared.
Column I: 1. a 500 g tiffin box on a shelf 80 cm high  2. a 2 kg bag on a hook 150 cm high  3. a 250 g ball at 4 m  4. a 40 kg boy on a platform 2.5 m high
Column II: a. 1000 J  b. 4 J  c. 30 J  d. 10 J
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-a. Convert to kg and m first: 4 J, 30 J, 10 J and 1000 J.

questions.q:
A fielder lobs a 150 g ball to 12 m above the ground. Take g = 10 m/s squared.
(a) Find its potential energy at the highest point.
(b) Find its kinetic energy just before it returns to the height from which it was thrown (ignore air resistance).
s: Part (b): mechanical energy is conserved, so the kinetic energy equals 18 J

questions.q:
A 40 kg student goes to a height of 54 m in a building, once in a lift and once by the stairs. Take g = 10 m/s squared.
(a) Find the gain in potential energy by the lift.
(b) Find it by the stairs and say what this shows about the path taken.
questions.a: (a) 21600 J. (b) 21600 J; the gain depends on the height, not the path.
s: Part (b): the same 21600 J, so it depends only on the height reached

questions.q: True or False? A 1 kg ball dropped from rest at 10 m has the same mechanical energy, 100 J, when it passes the 4 m mark (ignore air resistance), with 60 J of it kinetic energy. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. At 4 m the potential energy is 40 J, so the kinetic energy is 100 - 40 = 60 J.
s: Reason: mechanical energy is conserved, 40 J + 60 J = 100 J

questions.q: Why is the stored energy of the Earth-ball system often called simply the potential energy of the ball?
questions.a: The Earth is much more massive than the ball and hardly moves towards it, so the ball gains almost all of the kinetic energy.
s: Earth is much more massive than the ball
It hardly moves, so the energy shows up as the ball's motion

questions.q:
A catapult band is stretched and then released, shooting a pebble.
(a) Name the form of energy stored in the stretched band and why it is stored.
(b) Into what does it change when released?
questions.a: (a) Potential energy, stored by the deformation of the band. (b) Kinetic energy of the pebble.
s: Part (a): potential energy due to deformation
Part (b): kinetic energy of the pebble

questions.q: Ritu says, 'A heavier ball thrown up at 10 m/s goes higher than a lighter one, since it has more energy.' Check her claim (g = 10 m/s squared).
questions.a: No. Both reach 5 m: 1/2 mv^2 = mgh gives h = v^2 / 2g = 5 m, with m cancelling.

questions.q: A pendulum bob is released from 0.45 m above its lowest point. Show that, ignoring friction, it cannot swing up to 0.60 m above that point on the other side.
questions.a: Its mechanical energy is mg x 0.45, but at 0.60 m the potential energy alone would be mg x 0.60, which is more; kinetic energy cannot be negative.
s: Mechanical energy is conserved and equals mg x 0.45
Potential energy at 0.60 m is mg x 0.60, larger than the available energy
It can rise at most to 0.45 m

questions.q: Write a falling-object situation in which the object has a kinetic energy of 60 J just before landing. Give its mass and starting height and find its speed. Take g = 10 m/s squared.
questions.a: E.g. a 1.2 kg object dropped from 5 m: mgh = 60 J; 1/2 x 1.2 x v^2 = 60 gives v = 10 m/s.
s: A mass and height with mgh = 60 J
Kinetic energy just before landing equals mgh

questions.q: A pendulum bob of mass 0.2 kg is released at rest 1.25 m above its lowest point. Find (i) its mechanical energy and (ii) its speed at the lowest point (ignore friction; g = 10 m/s squared).
questions.a: 2.5 J and 5 m/s
s: At the lowest point all of it is kinetic
v = square root of (2 x 2.5 / 0.2) = 5 m/s

questions.q: A truck of mass 5000 kg moving at 54 km/h enters an escape ramp inclined at 30 degrees, where it rises 1 m for every 2 m along the ramp. The sand exerts a constant force of 25000 N against the motion. Take g = 10 m/s squared. Find (i) the speed in m/s, (ii) the initial kinetic energy, (iii) the potential energy after travelling d along the ramp, (iv) the work done by the sand, and (v) the minimum length of the ramp.
s: Height gained d/2, so potential energy = 5000 x 10 x d/2 = 25000 d

questions.q: A 2 kg coconut falls from the top of a 11.25 m tree onto wet sand and stops, making a depression. Take g = 10 m/s squared and assume all its energy goes into making the depression against an average resistive force of 5000 N. Find (i) the potential energy at the top, (ii) the kinetic energy just before it hits the sand, (iii) its speed then, (iv) the work done by the sand, and (v) the depth of the depression.
s: v = square root of (2 x 225 / 2) = 15 m/s

questions.q:
In a village in Uttarakhand a gharat (water mill) is fed by water that drops 5 m down a pipe before it strikes the wheel. Water flows at 20 kg every second. Take g = 10 m/s squared and ignore friction.
(a) Find the potential energy of 1 kg of water at the top.
(b) Find the speed of the water at the bottom of the pipe.
(c) Find the energy delivered to the wheel each second.
(d) The wheel needs the water to strike at 12 m/s or more. Plan 1 raises the pipe head to 10 m. Plan 2 doubles the flow to 40 kg per second. Which plan works? Show it.
questions.a: (a) 50 J (b) 10 m/s (c) 1000 J (d) Plan 1: speed 14.1 m/s; Plan 2 keeps 10 m/s although it also gives 2000 J each second.
s: v = square root of (2 x 10 x 5) = 10 m/s
Plan 1: v = 14.1 m/s, above 12; Plan 2: speed unchanged at 10 m/s, below 12

questions.q:
At a science park a 0.1 kg ball is released from rest at point A, 0.8 m above the lowest point B of a roller track. Take g = 10 m/s squared. At the next peak C, 0.55 m high, the ball is measured to move at 1 m/s.
(a) Find the mechanical energy at A.
(b) Find the speed at B if there were no friction.
(c) Find the mechanical energy at C and the energy lost by then.
(d) The students want the ball to cross a peak 0.9 m high, assuming the same loss of energy by then. Will releasing from 1.0 m be enough? Show it.
questions.a: (a) 0.8 J (b) 4 m/s (c) 0.6 J; 0.2 J lost (d) No: it needs 0.9 + 0.2 = 1.1 J, but 1.0 m gives 1.0 J; release from 1.1 m.
s: v = square root of (2 x 10 x 0.8) = 4 m/s
Needed 1.1 J exceeds 1.0 J, so not enough; 1.1 m is required

questions.q: A hostel motor lifts 50 kg of water through 12 m in 20 s. Taking g = 10 m/s squared, its average power is ___ W.
Asha and Bina, who have the same mass, climb the same flight of stairs. Asha runs up in 30 s and Bina walks up in 60 s. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Both do the same work, and Asha's power is twice Bina's. Work is the same; P = W / t is larger for the shorter time.
o: Both do the same work, and Asha's power is twice Bina's
Asha does twice the work and has twice the power
Both do the same work and have the same power
Bina does more work because she is on the stairs longer

questions.q: A motorbike and rider of total mass 200 kg start from rest and reach 36 km/h in 5 s. What average power does the engine supply?
Machine X does 6000 J of work in 20 s. Machine Y does 4500 J in 10 s. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Y has more power, 450 W against 300 W, though it does less work. P(X) = 300 W and P(Y) = 450 W.
o: Y has more power, 450 W against 300 W, though it does less work
X has more power, since it does the larger amount of work in total
X and Y have equal power, as both take a few seconds
Y has more power, 450 W against 600 W

questions.q: Meera writes the power of a pump in four ways. Which one CANNOT be a unit of power?
questions.a: N m (newton metre). 1 N m = 1 J, a unit of work; the others equal 1 W.
o: N m (newton metre)
J / s (joule per second)
N m / s (newton metre per second)
kg m^2 s^-3

questions.q: A crane lifts a mass m to the 10th floor in time t, then lifts the same mass to the 20th floor in 2t (all floors equal in height, starting from the ground). How does the power in the second job compare with that in the first?
questions.a: It is the same. Work doubles and time doubles, so W / t is unchanged.
o: It is the same
It is twice as much
It is half as much
It is four times as much

questions.q:
Statement 1: Doing the same work in less time needs more power.
Statement 2: An engine that does 600 J of work in 2 s has a power of 1200 W.
Statement 3: A machine that does more work always has more power.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only. Statement 2: 600 / 2 = 300 W. Statement 3 ignores the time taken.
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Running up a flight of stairs in one minute needs more power than walking up it in five minutes.
Reason (R): The same work is done in both cases.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. R is true, but the extra power comes from the shorter time for that work, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A 45 kg boy climbs a rope 4 m in 12 s. Take g = 10 m/s squared.
(a) Find the work done against gravity.
(b) Find his average power.

A 500 W pump runs for 3 minutes.
(a) How much energy does it transfer?
(b) What mass of water could it lift through 10 m with this energy (g = 10 m/s squared, no losses)?
True or False? A 1 kW motor and a 500 W motor each lift the same load through the same height; the 1 kW motor does twice the work. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The work is the same; the 1 kW motor works at twice the rate, so it takes half the time.
s: Correction: equal work, but power is the rate, so time halves

questions.q: Differentiate between work and power using the stair-climbing example.
questions.a: Work is the force times displacement and is the same for running or walking up; power is the rate of doing that work, greater when the time is shorter.
s: Work is the same in both climbs
Power is work divided by time, larger for the faster climb

questions.q:
A flag is raised from the ground to the top of a 12 m pole using a pulley.
(a) What determines the work done on the flag?
(b) How does the power change if the flag is raised at twice the speed?
questions.a: (a) The flag's weight and the height raised. (b) The power doubles.
s: Part (a): weight of the flag and height, not the speed
Part (b): same work in half the time, so power doubles

questions.q: Vikas says, 'Machine P lifts a load doing 2000 J of work in 4 s and Q does 1500 J in 2 s. P does more work so P has more power.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. P = 500 W and Q = 750 W, so Q has more power.

questions.q: A scooter and rider have mass 160 kg and reach a speed in a fixed time. A pillion rider of 40 kg joins, and the scooter reaches the same speed in the same time. Kiran says the fuel needed rises by 40%. Check this.
questions.a: No. Kinetic energy is proportional to mass, 200 / 160 = 1.25, so the fuel needed rises by 25%.
s: Fuel energy equals kinetic energy, proportional to the mass

questions.q: Show that a 400 W motor cannot lift a 50 kg load through 10 m in 10 s (g = 10 m/s squared, no losses).
questions.a: The work needed is 5000 J in 10 s, a power of 500 W, but the motor gives only 400 W (4000 J in 10 s).
s: 500 W is more than 400 W, so it is impossible

questions.q: Write a situation in which a machine has a power of 250 W. Give the work done and the time taken.
questions.a: E.g. a pump does 5000 J of work in 20 s: 5000 / 20 = 250 W.

questions.q: A crane lifts a 600 kg beam to the 10th floor, 30 m up, in 40 s, and later to the 20th floor, 60 m up, in 80 s. Find the work and the power for each lift (g = 10 m/s squared).
s: 180000 J in the first lift, 360000 J in the second
4500 W for the second, equal to the first

questions.q: A borewell fills a 3000 kg tank of water at a height of 10 m. Motor A is rated 750 W and motor B 1500 W. Take g = 10 m/s squared and ignore losses. (i) Find the work needed. (ii) Find the time taken by A. (iii) Find the time taken by B. (iv) Compare the energy used by each. (v) State which motor you would choose for a school and why.
questions.a: (i) 300000 J (ii) 400 s (iii) 200 s (iv) equal, 300000 J (v) a reasoned choice
s: Same energy; power only changes the speed
A choice with a reason such as time saved against rating or cost

questions.q: A bus of mass 4000 kg starts from rest and reaches 54 km/h in 12 s. (i) Convert the speed to m/s. (ii) Find the final kinetic energy. (iii) State the work done by the engine. (iv) Find the power. (v) Find the power if it reached the same speed in 6 s.
s: Work equals the change in kinetic energy, 450000 J

questions.q:
On a building site in Hyderabad a hoist lifts bricks of 3 kg each, 40 at a time, to a height of 15 m in 20 s. Take g = 10 m/s squared. 4800 bricks are to be lifted in 50 minutes of hoisting. A 900 W hoist costs Rs 1200 a day to hire and a 600 W hoist costs Rs 700 a day.
(a) Find the work and power for one batch.
(b) Find the time a 600 W hoist needs for one batch.
(c) Find the time each type needs for all the bricks.
(d) Decide what to hire if the work is done in one day.
questions.a: (a) 18000 J; 900 W (b) 30 s (c) 40 min and 60 min (d) A 900 W hoist (Rs 1200) meets 50 min; two 600 W hoists cost Rs 1400.
s: Only the 900 W hoist alone meets 50 min; two 600 W hoists cost Rs 1400 against Rs 1200

questions.q:
Ramesh's scooter has a mass of 100 kg and he has a mass of 60 kg. On Monday he reaches 36 km/h in 5 s. On Tuesday his son of 40 kg rides along and the scooter reaches the same speed in the same 5 s. Assume the energy comes entirely from fuel and there are no other losses.
(a) Find the kinetic energy reached on each day.
(b) Find the power on each day.
(c) Find the ratio of fuel used on Monday to Tuesday.
(d) Ramesh believes starting more gently, reaching the speed in 10 s on Tuesday, would save fuel. Is he right? Say what changes.
questions.a: (a) 8000 J and 10000 J (b) 1600 W and 2000 W (c) 4 : 5 (d) No: the energy is the same 10000 J; only the power falls to 1000 W.
s: Same 10000 J of energy, so no saving; only power halves to 1000 W

questions.q: A 600 N drum is rolled up a smooth plank 4.5 m long onto a platform 1.5 m high. Ignoring friction, the effort needed is ___ N.
A ramp is built over a step 24 cm high and the ramp's base is 32 cm wide. What is the mechanical advantage of the ramp?
questions.a: 1.67. The ramp length is 40 cm (right-angled triangle), so MA = L / h = 40 / 24; 1.33 uses the base instead of the length.

questions.q: A seesaw has seats A and B on the left, 2 m and 1 m from the fulcrum C, and seats D and E on the right, 1 m and 2 m from C. A 24 kg child sits at E. Where should a 48 kg child sit to balance?
questions.a: Seat B, 1 m left of the fulcrum. 24 kg x 2 m = 48 kg x L gives L = 1 m, on the opposite side.
o: Seat B, 1 m left of the fulcrum
Seat A, 2 m left of the fulcrum
Seat D, 1 m right of the fulcrum
Seat E, 2 m right of the fulcrum

questions.q: In a lemon squeezer the lemon is pressed at a point between the hinge and the point where the hand pushes. To which class of lever does it belong?
questions.a: Class II, with the load between the fulcrum and the effort. The chapter lists the lemon squeezer, wheelbarrow and bottle opener as Class II levers.
o: Class II, with the load between the fulcrum and the effort
Class I, with the fulcrum between the load and the effort
Class III, with the effort between the fulcrum and the load
It is not a lever, since it has a hinge

questions.q: Which statement about a fixed pulley is NOT correct?
questions.a: It gives a mechanical advantage greater than 1, so heavy loads need less effort. A fixed pulley has MA = 1; movable pulleys give MA greater than 1.
o: It gives a mechanical advantage greater than 1, so heavy loads need less effort
It changes only the direction of the effort
The effort and the load are equal in magnitude
It is easier to pull down on the rope than to lift the load upward

questions.q: A lever lifts a 90 N stone using a 30 N effort. The stone rises 0.1 m. How far does the effort end move?
questions.a: 0.3 m. F1 x d1 = F2 x d2 gives 30 x d1 = 90 x 0.1, so d1 = 0.3 m.
o: 3 m

questions.q:
Statement 1: A movable pulley system can have a mechanical advantage greater than 1.
Statement 2: Making the effort arm of a lever longer reduces the effort needed for the same load.
Statement 3: Using a longer ramp to reach the same height reduces the work done by the person, ignoring friction.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: the effort falls but acts over a longer distance, so the work stays the same.
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A lever can lift a load greater than the effort applied, yet the total work done is not reduced.
Reason (R): In every lever the effort arm is longer than the load arm.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. R is false: in a Class III lever the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load, so its arm is shorter.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Match each machine (column I) with its mechanical advantage (column II).
Column I: 1. a ramp 6 m long raising a load 1.5 m  2. a lever with effort arm 90 cm and load arm 30 cm  3. a fixed pulley  4. a ramp with base 16 cm and height 12 cm
Column II: a. 3  b. 1  c. 4  d. about 1.67
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d. 6 / 1.5 = 4; 90 / 30 = 3; a fixed pulley has 1; the ramp length is 20 cm so 20 / 12 = 1.67.

questions.q:
A 150 N load is lifted with a lever whose effort arm is 90 cm and load arm 30 cm.
(a) Find the mechanical advantage.
(b) Find the effort needed.

A hill road rises 60 m over a run of 600 m along the road.
(a) Find its mechanical advantage as an inclined plane.
(b) What does a driver pay for this gain?
questions.a: (a) 10. (b) A longer distance; the work done is the same.
s: Part (b): the force is smaller but acts over a longer distance

questions.q: True or False? Pushing a hard object closer to the fulcrum of scissors makes it easier to cut, because the load arm becomes smaller. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Mechanical advantage = effort arm / load arm, so a smaller load arm gives a larger advantage.
s: Reason: MA = effort arm / load arm rises as the load arm shortens

questions.q: Differentiate between a fixed pulley and a movable pulley system in their mechanical advantage and what they do.
questions.a: A fixed pulley has MA 1 and only changes the direction of the effort; a movable pulley system has MA greater than 1 and lifts heavy loads with smaller effort.
s: Fixed pulley: MA 1, direction change only
Movable system: MA greater than 1, smaller effort

questions.q:
In Activity 7.5 one coin (effort) hangs 10 cm from the fulcrum of a beam.
(a) How far from the fulcrum must 4 coins (load) hang to balance it?
(b) Find the mechanical advantage in this case.
s: Part (a): 1 x 10 = 4 x L gives 2.5 cm

questions.q: Gopal says, 'A longer ramp makes lifting easier because it reduces the work done.' Is he right?
questions.a: Partly. A longer ramp reduces the effort needed, but the work done is the same (ignoring friction).
s: True part: smaller force on a longer ramp
Wrong part: work is unchanged since the distance increases

questions.q: Mira says a lever with an effort arm of 1.2 m and a load arm of 0.4 m can lift a 90 N load with a 30 N effort. Check this.
questions.a: Yes. 30 x 1.2 = 36 and 90 x 0.4 = 36, so the effort balances the load.

questions.q: Show that a machine cannot lift a 200 N load through 2 m if the person does only 300 J of work on it (ignore friction).
questions.a: The useful work is 200 x 2 = 400 J, and machines do not create energy, so at least 400 J must be put in.
s: Work in cannot be less than work out

questions.q: Write a lever situation with mechanical advantage 4. Give the arm lengths and the effort for a 120 N load.
questions.a: E.g. effort arm 80 cm and load arm 20 cm: MA = 4, effort = 120 / 4 = 30 N.
s: Arm lengths giving a ratio of 4

questions.q: A 20 kg bag (g = 10 m/s squared) is raised 1.2 m onto a platform (a) by lifting it, (b) up a 6 m plank, (c) up a 3 m plank, ignoring friction. For each find the effort, the mechanical advantage and the work done, and then state what is gained and what is paid.
questions.a: (a) 200 N, MA 1, 240 J (b) 40 N, MA 5, 240 J (c) 80 N, MA 2.5, 240 J; effort falls but distance rises
s: What is paid: a longer distance

questions.q: On a seesaw a 60 kg adult sits 0.5 m from the fulcrum. (i) Where should a 25 kg child sit to balance? (ii) Find the mechanical advantage with the adult as the load. (iii) Name the class of lever. (iv) If the child moves to 0.6 m, which side goes down? (v) If the adult side drops 0.2 m, how far does the child side rise?
questions.a: (i) 1.2 m (ii) 2.4 (iii) Class I (iv) adult side (v) 0.48 m
s: Fulcrum between load and effort, Class I
Child moment 15 < adult moment 30, so the adult side goes down

questions.q:
A village in Himachal wants a ramp so that a 240 kg loaded handcart can be pushed onto a platform 1.5 m high (g = 10 m/s squared, ignore friction). A 3 m ramp costs Rs 4000 and a 6 m ramp costs Rs 7500. A worker can safely push at most 700 N, and an extra worker costs Rs 600 a day.
(a) Find the mechanical advantage of each ramp.
(b) Find the effort on each ramp.
(c) Show that the work done is the same.
(d) The job lasts 5 days. Which plan is cheaper, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) 2 and 4 (b) 1200 N and 600 N (c) 3600 J each (d) The 3 m ramp with two workers costs Rs 7000, Rs 500 less than Rs 7500.
s: 3 m ramp with two workers (600 N each): 4000 + 5 x 600 = Rs 7000, cheaper by Rs 500

questions.q:
In a school lab a beam is balanced on a fulcrum. One coin hangs on the left at 20 cm. On the right, 2 coins balance at 10 cm, 4 coins at 5 cm and 8 coins at 2.5 cm.
(a) Show that the number of coins times distance is constant for the right side.
(b) Find the mechanical advantage when 4 coins are the load.
(c) Predict the distance at which 10 coins would balance.
(d) Radha puts 10 coins 1.5 cm from the fulcrum. Which side goes down and by how much in coin-cm, and where should the coins go?
questions.a: (a) 20 each (b) 4 (c) 2 cm (d) The left (effort) side goes down by 5 coin-cm; move the load to 2 cm.
s: 10 x 1.5 = 15 is less than 20, so the effort side goes down by 5; move to 2 cm
